what_it_does: When a large language model generates text, it produces one word (or token) at a time, and each new word requires the model to look back at everything it has generated so far. This look-back involves reading a large table of stored context — keys and values for every past position — from memory. As a conversation grows beyond roughly 2,000 words, this memory-reading step alone consumes more than half of the total generation time on a GPU. The LAD chip (a custom-built hardware accelerator, meaning a chip designed specifically for this task rather than a general-purpose processor) attacks the problem by noticing that the score the model assigns to a given past position often stays nearly the same across several consecutive generation steps. When a score is stable, the chip's detection logic marks that position as 'settled' and stops re-reading its data on every step, dramatically cutting the number of memory accesses. A small on-chip score-history buffer tracks past scores to make this detection reliable, and the chip's specialized arithmetic units for the attention computation are designed to work seamlessly with the skipping logic.
